situation: Objective: find why a cinema chain's profit fell $3M this year. What you've learned: revenue was flat across its 30 cinemas. Latest finding: snack and drink sales, which earn most of the margin, fell 20%.
new_fact: Ticket sales are flat, but the share of moviegoers who buy snacks fell from 60% to 45% after the chain raised snack prices in March.
model_answer_stage1: Break snack and drink sales into moviegoers, the share who buy and spend per buyer, by month, since the 20% fall in high-margin snacks likely explains most of the $3M.
model_answer_stage2: Keep: tickets are flat but fewer moviegoers buy snacks since the March price rise, so I'd look at snack buying before and after the price change.

situation: Objective: get a regional airline's flights leaving on time again. What you've learned: flights now leave 25 minutes late on average, up from 8 minutes last year. Latest finding: most of the delay is at its two busiest airports, which handle 60% of flights.
new_fact: At those two airports, turning a plane around between flights now takes 65 minutes, up from 45, since a new ground-handling contractor took over in the spring.
model_answer_stage1: Compare how long each turnaround step, such as cleaning, fueling and boarding, takes at the two busiest airports this year against last, since most of the delay now starts there.
model_answer_stage2: Keep: turnarounds there rose from 45 to 65 minutes after the new contractor took over, so I'd find which steps the contractor does more slowly.

situation: Objective: decide whether a US maker of premium baby strollers should enter Canada. What you've learned: Canada's premium stroller market is about $150M a year and growing 8%. Latest finding: two local brands hold 70% of it.
new_fact: Most premium strollers in Canada are sold through about 300 independent baby stores, and the two local brands have exclusive deals with 240 of them.
model_answer_stage1: Find out how Canadians buy premium strollers, through which stores or sites, and whether the two local brands control those channels, since they hold 70% of the market.
model_answer_stage2: Keep: the local brands have exclusive deals with 240 of the 300 stores that sell most strollers, so I'd test whether online or the other 60 stores could carry us.

situation: Objective: cut the energy bill of a chain of 40 indoor ice rinks by 10%, from $12M a year. What you've learned: its energy prices are fixed by contract until 2028. Latest finding: making and cooling the ice uses half of all the energy.
new_fact: Most rinks keep the ice at the same temperature around the clock, though they sit empty about 10 hours a day. The five rinks that let the ice warm slightly overnight use 25% less energy on it.
model_answer_stage1: Break the ice plant's energy use down by rink and by hour of the day, since making and cooling the ice uses half of the $12M bill.
model_answer_stage2: Keep: the five rinks that warm the ice overnight use 25% less on it, so I'd size that saving across the other 35 rinks against the $1.2M target.

situation: Objective: grow revenue 15% next year at a chain of 25 craft-supply stores. What you've learned: revenue per store has been flat for two years. Latest finding: loyalty-card members spend three times as much a year as other shoppers.
new_fact: Only 20% of shoppers are members, and the stores whose cashiers offer the card at every checkout sign up twice as many shoppers as the others.
model_answer_stage1: Compare how many shoppers are loyalty members, and how they're signed up, store by store, since members spend three times as much as other shoppers.
model_answer_stage2: Keep: only 20% are members and asking at every checkout doubles sign-ups, so I'd estimate the revenue from rolling that out to all 25 stores.

situation: Objective: decide whether a hotel-linen laundry company should buy a smaller rival for $60M. What you've learned: the rival would add $50M of revenue. Latest finding: the rival's profit margin is 4%, against the client's 11%.
new_fact: The rival's low margin comes from running two half-empty plants, and the client's nearest plant has 40% spare capacity.
model_answer_stage1: Compare the rival's costs per pound of linen with ours, line by line, since its 4% margin against our 11% decides whether the $60M buys a business we can fix.
model_answer_stage2: Keep: half-empty plants explain the margin, so I'd go a level deeper: size the savings from moving the rival's volume into our nearby plant, with 40% spare capacity.

situation: Objective: find why a cereal maker's new high-protein granola sold 40% below plan in its first six months. What you've learned: shoppers who try it rate it highly. Latest finding: 70% of stores shelve it with diet and health foods, not with the cereals.
new_fact: In the 30% of stores that shelve it with the cereals, it sells at plan.
model_answer_stage1: Compare sales per store where the granola sits with the cereals against stores that shelve it with diet foods, since 70% of stores keep it away from cereal shoppers.
model_answer_stage2: Keep: it sells at plan where it sits with the cereals, so I'd find out what it would take to move it there in the other 70% of stores.

situation: Objective: win back visitors to a city's botanical garden, whose visits fell 18% in two years. What you've learned: school-group visits held steady. Latest finding: family visits on Saturdays and Sundays fell 38%.
new_fact: Two years ago the garden began closing at 2pm on Saturdays and Sundays instead of 6pm to save staff costs, and visits in the hours still open held steady.
model_answer_stage1: Compare Saturday and Sunday family visits by hour over the two years with the garden's opening times and events on those days, since that is where the fall is.
model_answer_stage2: Keep: closing moved from 6pm to 2pm on those days, and visits in the open hours held, so I'd weigh the staff cost of reopening afternoons against visits regained.

situation: Objective: find why a chain of 20 dog-grooming salons' profit fell 30% this year. What you've learned: revenue held steady. Latest finding: water and energy cost per groom rose 40%.
new_fact: The chain replaced its bathing stations in the spring, and the new stations use twice the water per bath; utility prices were flat.
model_answer_stage1: Compare water and energy used per groom this year against last, salon by salon, since cost per groom rose 40% and how much each groom uses is the likeliest driver.
model_answer_stage2: Keep: the new stations use twice the water per bath at flat prices, so I'd size the cost of the extra water against adjusting or replacing them.

situation: Objective: cut how long an insurer takes to settle car-damage claims. What you've learned: claims now take 30 days to settle, up from 18. Latest finding: the number of claims is flat.
new_fact: Claims that need a garage's repair estimate now wait 15 days for it, up from 3, since the insurer switched to a new network of garages.
model_answer_stage1: Map how long a claim spends at each step, such as the repair estimate, review and payment, this year against last, since claims are flat but take 12 days longer.
model_answer_stage2: Keep: the estimate step alone went from 3 days to 15 after the switch to new garages, so I'd compare estimate times across the new garages.

situation: Objective: grow revenue 10% next year at a chain of 15 kitchenware stores. What you've learned: store sales have been flat for two years. Latest finding: cooking classes held in the stores grew 40%, and class students spend twice as much on kitchenware.
new_fact: Class students spent twice as much before their first class too, but the chain sells almost nothing online, where half of all kitchenware is now bought.
model_answer_stage1: Compare yearly kitchenware spending by class students and other shoppers, store by store, since class students spend twice as much and classes grew 40%.
model_answer_stage2: Change: class students spent twice as much before their first class, so classes don't raise spending; I'd size the revenue from selling online, where half of kitchenware is bought.

situation: Objective: raise the share of homeowners who pay a county's property tax on time. What you've learned: on-time payment fell from 92% to 80% this year. Latest finding: almost all the drop is among homeowners who used to pay by mailed check.
new_fact: This year the county stopped mailing paper bills and sends them only by email; homeowners without an email address on file got no bill at all.
model_answer_stage1: Find out what changed this year for homeowners who pay by check, such as how their bills reach them or where they mail payments, since nearly all the drop is among them.
model_answer_stage2: Keep: the county stopped mailing paper bills, and homeowners without an email on file got none, so I'd count them and restart paper bills for them.

situation: Objective: decide whether a Swedish maker of electric kettles should start selling in France. What you've learned: France's kettle market is about €150M a year. Latest finding: French shoppers buy most kettles online, through two large websites.
new_fact: Both websites list any brand that meets EU safety rules, as the client's kettles do, and their best-selling kettles cost under €40, half the client's price.
model_answer_stage1: Find out what it takes to get listed on the two big websites, such as their terms, fees and rules for new brands, since most French kettles sell through them.
model_answer_stage2: Change: any brand meeting EU rules gets listed, so I'd compare the client's price and features with the best-selling kettles, which cost under €40, half of ours.

situation: Objective: cut a law firm's office costs by 12%. What you've learned: office costs are $5M a year. Latest finding: printing makes up 25% of them, up from 8% five years ago.
new_fact: Pages printed haven't changed in five years; the cost rose because a printer lease signed three years ago charges four times the market price per page.
model_answer_stage1: Break printing costs down by department and type of document, this year against five years ago, since printing tripled as a share of office costs.
model_answer_stage2: Change: pages printed are flat but the lease charges four times the market price per page, so I'd cost moving to a lease at market rates.

situation: Objective: find why a toy maker's new building set sold 50% below plan in its first holiday season. What you've learned: buyers gave it top ratings. Latest finding: it sold out in most stores by early December.
new_fact: The factory made only half the units planned, and stores couldn't restock until January.
model_answer_stage1: Compare the units made and shipped to stores with the plan, week by week through December, since the set sold out early and still sold below plan.
model_answer_stage2: Keep: the factory made half the planned units and stores couldn't restock, so I'd find what limited production and fix it before next season.

situation: Objective: return a chain of 20 hardware stores to profit after two years of losses. What you've learned: the losses come from 6 stores opened in the last three years. Latest finding: the 6 new stores sell half as much per square foot as the older ones.
new_fact: The 6 new stores draw as many shoppers as the older ones, but only half of those shoppers buy anything, and the new stores carry 40% fewer products.
model_answer_stage1: Compare foot traffic at the 6 new stores with the older ones, month by month, since they sell half as much per square foot.
model_answer_stage2: Change: the new stores draw as many shoppers, but only half buy and they carry 40% fewer products, so I'd compare their range with the older stores'.

situation: Objective: decide whether a regional theater should raise ticket prices. What you've learned: shows are 97% sold out at weekends and 55% on weekdays. Latest finding: weekend tickets sell out two months ahead.
new_fact: Resale websites sell the theater's weekend tickets at twice face value.
model_answer_stage1: Estimate how much weekend buyers would pay, for example from how fast each price band sells, since weekend shows sell out two months ahead.
model_answer_stage2: Keep: resale sites sell weekend tickets at twice face value, so buyers will pay more; I'd test a weekend price rise of 15–25%.

situation: Objective: respond to a new rival taking customers from a regional internet provider. What you've learned: the client lost 8% of its customers this year. Latest finding: the losses are almost all in the three towns where the rival laid fiber.
new_fact: In those towns the rival matches the client's speeds and prices, and customers who left mostly cite outages, which tripled there this year.
model_answer_stage1: Compare what the rival offers in the three towns with the client's plans, speed and price side by side, since nearly all the losses are there.
model_answer_stage2: Change: the offers match on speed and price, and leavers cite outages, which tripled, so I'd find what is causing the outages in those three towns.

situation: Objective: find why a chain of 40 pharmacies' profit fell $6M this year. What you've learned: prescriptions filled rose 5%. Latest finding: profit per prescription fell 25%.
new_fact: Two large insurers cut what they pay pharmacies per prescription by 30% in January; together they cover 60% of the chain's customers.
model_answer_stage1: Compare what the chain pays to buy its most-filled drugs this year against last, since profit per prescription fell 25% while volume rose.
model_answer_stage2: Change: two insurers covering 60% of customers cut payments 30%, so I'd look at payments by insurer and whether the chain can renegotiate.

situation: Objective: cut wrong-item shipments at an office-supplies distributor, which rose from 1% to 4% of orders this year. What you've learned: order volume rose 10%. Latest finding: most errors happen on the night shift.
new_fact: The night shift is mostly temporary workers hired this year, and they skip the barcode scan at packing twice as often as day staff.
model_answer_stage1: Compare error rates by shift and by worker, this year against last, since most wrong-item shipments now happen on the night shift.
model_answer_stage2: Keep: night-shift temps skip the barcode scan twice as often, so I'd check their training and whether packing can block unscanned items.

situation: Objective: decide whether a Canadian maple-syrup brand should start selling in Japan. What you've learned: Japan imports about $40M of maple syrup a year. Latest finding: most of it is sold to bakeries and cafés, not in supermarkets.
new_fact: Bakeries and cafés buy only the cheapest grade, at prices 40% below the client's cost to land it in Japan, while premium syrup in supermarkets grew 30% last year.
model_answer_stage1: Find out how bakeries and cafés buy maple syrup, through which suppliers and at what prices, since most of Japan's imports go to them rather than supermarkets.
model_answer_stage2: Change: bakeries buy the cheapest grade at 40% below our landed cost, so I'd size premium syrup in supermarkets, which grew 30% last year.

situation: Objective: cut a home insurer's call-center costs by 20%. What you've learned: calls rose 35% in two years while customers rose 5%. Latest finding: 40% of calls are customers asking about the status of a claim.
new_fact: The insurer's website and app don't show claim status, so customers can only get it by calling.
model_answer_stage1: Break claim-status calls down by claim type and how long each claim has been open, since they are 40% of calls and drive most of the rise.
model_answer_stage2: Keep: claim status isn't shown online, so customers must call; I'd estimate the calls saved by showing it in the app.

situation: Objective: grow a regional ice-cream maker's sales 15% in two years. What you've learned: sales to restaurants are flat. Latest finding: grocery-store sales grew 30% this year, but the brand is in only 20% of the region's grocery stores.
new_fact: Grocery stores that stock the brand sell out in most weeks, and its plant already runs at full capacity.
model_answer_stage1: Estimate sales if the brand reached more of the region's grocery stores, using sales per store where it is stocked today, since grocery sales grew 30%.
model_answer_stage2: Change: the plant is already at full capacity, so I'd size the cost of more capacity first, since new stores can't be supplied without it.

situation: Objective: decide whether a software company should move from one price to three tiers. What you've learned: it charges $30 per user a month to every customer. Latest finding: small customers cancel at three times the rate of large ones, citing price.
new_fact: Small customers use only 2 of the product's 10 features, while large customers use 8.
model_answer_stage1: Compare which features small and large customers use and what each would pay, since small customers cancel three times as often, citing price.
model_answer_stage2: Keep: small customers use 2 of 10 features against large customers' 8, so I'd price a basic tier around those 2 features.

situation: Objective: decide whether a chain of 30 veterinary clinics should buy a rival chain of 10 for $25M. What you've learned: the rival earns $2.5M a year. Latest finding: 40% of the rival's revenue comes from one clinic.
new_fact: That clinic is the region's only 24-hour emergency hospital, with steady visits for ten years, while the rival's other nine clinics lost money last year.
model_answer_stage1: Find out why one clinic brings in 40% of the rival's revenue, such as its location or its vets, since the $25M price depends on that clinic.
model_answer_stage2: Change: the big clinic is a steady, one-of-a-kind emergency hospital, so I'd find why the other nine clinics lost money and whether the client could fix them.

situation: Objective: cut the backlog of tax refunds at a state revenue agency. What you've learned: the backlog doubled to 40,000 in six months, while returns filed rose 8%. Latest finding: refunds flagged for identity checks take 30 days, against 5 for the rest.
new_fact: Since a new fraud rule in March, 60% of refunds are flagged for identity checks, up from 10%, and almost none of the newly flagged refunds turn out to be fraud.
model_answer_stage1: Compare staff hours spent on identity checks with the number of flagged refunds, month by month, since flagged refunds take 30 days against 5 for the rest.
model_answer_stage2: Change: the new rule flags 60% of refunds and almost none are fraud, so I'd look at narrowing what gets flagged before adding staff.

situation: Objective: find why a cosmetics brand's new sunscreen missed its first-summer sales target by 30%. What you've learned: sales were on plan in May and June. Latest finding: sales fell 55% in July and August, the busiest months.
new_fact: After a rival's sunscreen was recalled in July, stores pulled every sunscreen with the same active ingredient, the client's included, for six weeks.
model_answer_stage1: Compare July and August sales store by store with how much stock each store held, since sales fell 55% in the busiest months after a good start.
model_answer_stage2: Keep: stores pulled sunscreens with that ingredient for six weeks, so I'd estimate the sales lost and how to stay on shelves next summer.

situation: Objective: assess whether the dog-daycare industry is attractive to a private-equity investor. What you've learned: industry revenue grew 15% a year for five years. Latest finding: the three largest operators hold only 10% of the market.
new_fact: Most daycares are single sites run by their owners, and several regional operators have grown by buying them at about four times yearly profit.
model_answer_stage1: Estimate whether 15% growth will last, for example from dog ownership and how many owners work away from home, since with the top three holding only 10%, there's room to enter if demand keeps growing.
model_answer_stage2: Change: owners sell single sites at about four times profit, so I'd assess buying and combining them, and what a combined chain could earn.

situation: Objective: respond to a rival grocery-delivery service that cut its delivery fee to zero. What you've learned: the client's orders fell 12% in the month since. Latest finding: the losses are almost all among customers who order less than once a month.
new_fact: The client's weekly customers, who place 70% of its orders, kept ordering at the same rate.
model_answer_stage1: Compare how much the occasional customers who left spent with the client, and what they ordered, since nearly all the lost orders came from them.
model_answer_stage2: Keep: weekly customers placing 70% of orders stayed, so I'd size what the occasional ones are worth before matching free delivery for anyone.

situation: Objective: decide whether a tennis club should build indoor courts for $3M. What you've learned: the club has 900 members, and membership has been flat for five years. Latest finding: 60% of members who quit say they had nowhere to play in winter.
new_fact: A sports center nearby opened four indoor courts last year, and they are booked only half the time in winter.
model_answer_stage1: Survey members who quit in the last two years about whether they'd return for winter play, and at what fee, since 60% cite having nowhere to play in winter.
model_answer_stage2: Keep: courts nearby sit half empty in winter, so the survey may overstate demand; I'd test whether members who quit would actually pay for winter court time, and how much.

situation: Objective: find why an architecture firm's profit margin fell from 16% to 7%, though revenue grew 25%. What you've learned: staff costs rose faster than revenue. Latest finding: the share of staff hours billed to clients fell from 75% to 62%.
new_fact: Billed hours fell mostly on fixed-price projects, which went from 20% to 50% of revenue and ran 30% over their hour budgets.
model_answer_stage1: Break unbilled hours down by team and reason, such as admin, training or waiting for work, this year against last, since billed hours fell from 75% to 62%.
model_answer_stage2: Change: the drop comes from fixed-price projects running 30% over budget, so I'd compare how those projects are estimated with their actual hours.

situation: Objective: raise an auto-parts factory's output 15% without new machines. What you've learned: machines run 85% of their scheduled hours. Latest finding: 60% of the lost hours come from changeovers between product types.
new_fact: The factory switched from long runs to small daily batches last year to cut inventory, which tripled the number of changeovers.
model_answer_stage1: Time each changeover step on the main lines and compare it with industry benchmarks, since changeovers cause 60% of the lost machine hours.
model_answer_stage2: Change: changeovers tripled when batches got smaller, so how often lines switch matters more than how long each switch takes; I'd weigh larger batches against the inventory they'd add.

situation: Objective: decide whether a US chain of indoor go-kart tracks should open in São Paulo. What you've learned: São Paulo has 3 indoor tracks for 12 million people. Latest finding: the 3 tracks are full at weekends and charge about $30 a race, near US prices.
new_fact: Warehouse space large enough for a track costs three times as much as in the chain's US cities and takes 18 months to permit.
model_answer_stage1: Estimate how many residents would race regularly, for example from the 3 tracks' bookings and waiting lists, since they're full at weekends at near-US prices.
model_answer_stage2: Change: track-sized space costs three times US rents and takes 18 months to permit, so I'd check whether a track still pays back at those costs.

situation: Objective: decide whether a hotel-booking software company should buy a smaller rival for $80M. What you've learned: the rival's revenue grew 40% last year. Latest finding: 70% of the rival's customers also use the client's software.
new_fact: In a survey, shared customers say they use the two products for different jobs and would keep both; the rival's growth came from a payments feature 60% of its customers took up this year.
model_answer_stage1: Estimate how much of the rival's revenue would be new to the client, given that 70% of its customers already use the client's software, before judging the $80M price.
model_answer_stage2: Change: shared customers would keep both products, so the overlap costs little; I'd check whether the payments feature behind the 40% growth can keep growing.

situation: Objective: cut a regional grocery chain's shrink (stock lost to waste and theft) by a third. What you've learned: shrink is 4% of sales, against 2% for peers. Latest finding: fresh produce accounts for 60% of shrink.
new_fact: Stores order produce by hand each morning; the stores that over-order most throw away twice as much, and computer ordering halved produce waste in a 5-store pilot.
model_answer_stage1: Break produce shrink down by store and by cause, such as spoilage, damage or theft, since produce is 60% of a shrink rate twice the peers'.
model_answer_stage2: Change: stores that over-order waste twice as much, and computer ordering halved waste in a pilot, so I'd size rolling computer ordering out to every store.

situation: Objective: decide the price of a coworking company's new private-office membership. What you've learned: its desk membership costs $300 a month. Latest finding: rivals charge $800 to $1,200 a month for a private office.
new_fact: In a survey, 60% of the client's desk members who'd want a private office say they'd pay at most $600 a month.
model_answer_stage1: Compare what rivals' $800 to $1,200 offices include, such as size, location and services, with what the client could offer, since that sets where its price can sit.
model_answer_stage2: Change: 60% of interested members would pay at most $600, so I'd check whether offices pay back at $600, and who else would pay more.

situation: Objective: double a regional insurance broker's revenue in five years. What you've learned: 80% of revenue comes from small businesses. Latest finding: small-business clients hold one policy on average, against three at rival brokers.
new_fact: The gap is workers' compensation, which brokers in other states sell but which the client's state requires small businesses to buy from a state fund; new small businesses in the region grow 8% a year.
model_answer_stage1: Compare which policies the client's small-business customers hold with rivals' customers, by industry, since the client sells one policy each against rivals' three.
model_answer_stage2: Change: the policy gap is workers' compensation, which only the state fund may sell here, so I'd size winning new small businesses, which grow 8% a year.

situation: Objective: return a chain of 50 restaurants to profit; it loses $5M a year. What you've learned: sales per restaurant fell 15% in two years. Latest finding: online reviews mention slow service three times as often as two years ago.
new_fact: Two years ago the chain cut kitchen staff by 20% to save costs, and the average wait for food rose from 15 to 28 minutes.
model_answer_stage1: Compare wait times and staffing per shift with two years ago, restaurant by restaurant, since reviews mention slow service three times as often as sales fell.
model_answer_stage2: Keep: kitchen staff were cut 20% and waits rose from 15 to 28 minutes, so I'd compare the savings with the sales lost since.

situation: Objective: decide whether a distribution center should build four more loading docks for $20M. What you've learned: its 12 docks are 90% busy. Latest finding: trucks waited an average of 3 hours for a dock last year, up from 30 minutes.
new_fact: Half of the waiting comes from trucks that arrive outside their booked slot; trucks that keep their slot wait under 20 minutes.
model_answer_stage1: Estimate what four more docks would save in truck waiting and missed deliveries, against their $20M cost, since waits rose from 30 minutes to 3 hours.
model_answer_stage2: Change: half the waiting comes from trucks arriving outside their slot, so I'd first see how far stricter booking cuts waits before spending $20M.

situation: Objective: assess whether language-learning apps are an attractive market for a new entrant. What you've learned: the market grew 20% a year. Latest finding: two apps hold 75% of users.
new_fact: The two leaders spend about $100 to win each paying user, who pays about $60 a year and stays about two years.
model_answer_stage1: Find out how the two leaders won 75% of users, such as marketing spend or free features, since a new entrant would have to take users from them.
model_answer_stage2: Change: the leaders spend $100 to win a user worth about $120 over two years, so I'd check whether an entrant could win users more cheaply than that.
